name: Mast Cell Activation Syndrome

prevalence.estimate: Disputed; estimated 1-17% depending on diagnostic criteria used
prevalence.range: Conservative estimates ~1 per 10,000; broader criteria suggest much higher

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Consensus-2 Criteria (Valent et al. 2020) and Afrin/Molderings criteria

criteria.description: Episodic symptoms consistent with mast cell mediator release affecting two or more organ systems (skin, GI, cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological)

Elevated serum tryptase during a symptomatic episode: increase of at least 20% + 2 ng/mL above the patient's baseline, or other mast cell mediators elevated (urinary histamine metabolites, prostaglandin D2, leukotriene E4)
Response to medications targeting mast cell mediators (H1/H2 antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, leukotriene inhibitors)
Exclusion of other conditions that could explain the symptoms
KIT D816V mutation absent (distinguishes from systemic mastocytosis)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: All four major criteria must be met per consensus criteria. Afrin/Molderings criteria are broader and accept response to mast cell-directed therapy as supportive evidence even without documented mediator elevation.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Significant controversy exists regarding diagnostic criteria. Consensus-2 criteria (Valent) require biochemical evidence of mast cell mediator release. Afrin/Molderings criteria are broader. The two approaches yield very different prevalence estimates.

rare.notes: From chronic mediator release effects on bone

laboratory: Serum tryptase: elevated during episode (>=20% + 2 ng/mL above baseline)
24-hour urine prostaglandin D2 or 11-beta-prostaglandin F2-alpha elevated
Plasma heparin or chromogranin A may be elevated
imaging: DEXA scan may show reduced bone density in chronic cases
genetic: KIT D816V mutation absent (distinguishes from mastocytosis)
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (TPSAB1 extra copies) may coexist
other: Bone marrow biopsy: normal or near-normal mast cell morphology and number (distinguishes from mastocytosis)
Skin biopsy during flushing may show mast cell degranulation

distinguishingFeatures: Systemic mastocytosis has KIT D816V mutation in most cases
Systemic mastocytosis has abnormal mast cell aggregates on bone marrow biopsy
Baseline tryptase is persistently >20 ng/mL in mastocytosis
HaT has elevated baseline tryptase due to extra TPSAB1 gene copies
HaT is a genetic condition, not an episodic mast cell activation disorder
Idiopathic anaphylaxis presents with acute anaphylactic episodes
MCAS is broader with chronic episodic multisystem symptoms
Carcinoid flushing is typically dry, MCAS flushing may have urticaria

redFlags: Anaphylaxis without identifiable trigger (consider mast cell disorder workup)
Persistently elevated baseline tryptase >20 ng/mL (evaluate for systemic mastocytosis)
Bone marrow findings suggestive of clonal mast cell disease
Osteoporosis in a young patient with mast cell symptoms
references: Valent P, et al. Proposed diagnostic algorithm for patients with suspected mast cell activation syndrome. J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract. 2019;7(4):1125-1133.
Afrin LB, et al. Diagnosis of mast cell activation syndrome: a global 'consensus-2'. Diagnosis (Berl). 2021;8(2):137-152.
Weiler CR, et al. AAAAI Mast Cell Disorders Committee Work Group Report: Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) diagnosis and management. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2019;144(4):883-896.
